openingLine: Afternoon, doc. I'm Sam. They told me to come see you about my gallbladder.

rounds.prompt: Sam is pain-free and relaxed. What do you do next?

choices.text: Ask him to describe the attacks: when they started, how often, and what sets them off
choices.feedback: Recurrent attacks over months, triggered by fatty meals and settling within hours, are the core of biliary colic and justify elective surgery.
choices.patientCue: Attacks of pain up under my right ribs, mostly after dinner. About six months now, five or six of them, the last one two weeks ago. Fried food or a big dinner sets it off, and it goes away on its own in an hour or two.

choices.text: Tell him the gallbladder needs to come out and start the consent form
choices.feedback: Recommending surgery before hearing his story skips the history that justifies it.
choices.patientCue: Hold on, doc. You haven't even asked me what's been going on yet.

choices.text: Ask where the pain is and whether it spreads anywhere
choices.feedback: Location and shoulder spread are useful, but timing, frequency and triggers tell you more about colic versus cholecystitis.
choices.patientCue: Right side, under the ribs. Sometimes it goes up to my right shoulder.

choices.text: Ask about his family history of cancer
choices.feedback: Family history is low yield before you understand the presenting complaint.
choices.patientCue: Nothing I know of. But that's not why I came in, doc.

rounds.prompt: The attacks sound like a recurring pattern. What do you do next?

choices.text: Ask whether he could be pregnant
choices.feedback: Pregnancy does not apply to this patient, and the question wastes a chance to screen for complications.
choices.patientCue: He laughs. Doc, I'm a guy.

choices.text: Ask how his appetite has been
choices.feedback: Appetite is reasonable to ask, but it does not screen for cholecystitis or a duct stone the way fever and urine color do.
choices.patientCue: Fine between attacks.

choices.text: Ask about fevers, vomiting, dark urine and pale or bloody stools
choices.feedback: No fever, vomiting, dark urine or pale stools points away from cholecystitis, cholangitis and a common duct stone.
choices.patientCue: No fevers, no chills. I feel queasy during the attacks but I've never thrown up. Urine's normal, never dark, and my bowels are normal, no pale stools, no blood.

choices.text: Ask whether he has had any recent colds or infections
choices.feedback: Recent illness does not help separate simple colic from its complications.
choices.patientCue: No, I've been fine.

rounds.prompt: His chart shows no name, no birth date and no problem list. What do you do next?

choices.text: Confirm his name and date of birth in person, then ask about his medical problems, past surgery and anesthesia, and smoking
choices.feedback: Partial consent means unknown, not none, so identity and the problem list must come from him directly before any procedure.
choices.patientCue: Sam Ortiz. March twelfth, 1965. Good, that's how it should be. High blood pressure and high cholesterol, no heart attacks, no lung problems, no diabetes that I know of, and an open hernia repair on the right about fifteen years ago with no anesthesia problems. I quit smoking ten years ago after about thirty years of a pack a day.

choices.text: Request his full record from the health system so you can see everything
choices.feedback: He chose to share only medications and allergies, so working around his consent is wrong when you can simply ask him.
choices.patientCue: Tell you the truth, doc, I didn't share it on purpose. Ask me, I'll tell you.

choices.text: Ask what medical problems he has
choices.feedback: The problem list is essential, but skipping identity confirmation leaves the chart unable to say who this patient is.
choices.patientCue: High blood pressure and high cholesterol. No heart attacks, no lung problems, no diabetes that I know of. I only let them see my medicines and allergies.

choices.text: Document no past medical history since none is listed
choices.feedback: An empty problem list under partial consent is missing data, not a healthy patient.
choices.patientCue: Right, because I didn't share it. Ask me.

rounds.prompt: The chart lists lisinopril, atorvastatin and a penicillin allergy. What do you do next?

choices.text: Note the penicillin allergy and plan to give no antibiotic at surgery
choices.feedback: A penicillin label should be characterized, not used to skip prophylaxis.
choices.patientCue: Okay, doc. Whatever you think is safe.

choices.text: Ask what happened when he took penicillin
choices.feedback: Characterizing the allergy is key, but you also need to confirm the medication list is complete.
choices.patientCue: Penicillin gave me a rash when I was in the army. No swelling, no breathing trouble. Nothing since.

choices.text: Tell him to stop his cholesterol pill now
choices.feedback: Atorvastatin is continued around surgery and there is no reason to stop it.
choices.patientCue: Stop it? My regular doctor wants me on it. Why would I stop?

choices.text: Confirm the medication list is complete, including over-the-counter drugs, and ask exactly what the penicillin reaction was
choices.feedback: This confirms a complete list and shows a remote mild rash, which still allows cefazolin prophylaxis.
choices.patientCue: Lisinopril 10 in the morning and atorvastatin 20 at night. Maybe an ibuprofen once a month for a sore back. Penicillin gave me a rash in the army, no swelling, no breathing trouble, nothing since.

rounds.prompt: There are no vitals on his chart. What do you do next?

choices.text: Take a full set of vital signs and note his general appearance
choices.feedback: With no vitals on the chart, a baseline is needed before an elective operation.
choices.patientCue: Sure, doc.

finding.label: Vital signs
finding.text: Temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 76, blood pressure 138/84, respiratory rate 14, oxygen saturation 97% on room air.

choices.text: Look at his eyes and skin for yellowing
choices.feedback: Checking for jaundice is useful, but it does not replace the baseline vitals the chart lacks.
choices.patientCue: Sure, doc.

finding.label: General appearance
finding.text: Well appearing and comfortable. No jaundice or scleral icterus.

choices.text: Tap over his back for kidney tenderness
choices.feedback: Costovertebral angle tenderness is a kidney sign and does not address the missing baseline.
choices.patientCue: No.

choices.text: Skip vitals because he is pain-free and looks well
choices.feedback: Looking well is not a set of vital signs, and none are on file.
choices.patientCue: Okay, if you say so, doc.

rounds.prompt: His vitals are normal. What do you do next?

choices.text: Press on the lower right side of his belly
choices.feedback: Right lower quadrant tenderness is an appendicitis sign and does not fit his story.
choices.patientCue: Nothing there.

finding.label: Right lower quadrant
finding.text: Nontender in the right lower quadrant.

choices.text: Gently palpate his whole abdomen
choices.feedback: Palpation is right, but without a Murphy sign you have not excluded acute cholecystitis.
choices.patientCue: That's alright. A little tender up on the right, but not like an attack.

finding.label: Abdominal palpation
finding.text: Soft. Minimal right upper quadrant tenderness to deep palpation, no guarding, no mass.

choices.text: Palpate the abdomen, then press under the right ribs while he breathes in to check a Murphy sign
choices.feedback: A soft abdomen with a negative Murphy sign between attacks supports uncomplicated gallstones over cholecystitis.
choices.patientCue: That's alright. A little tender up on the right, but not like an attack. No, I can breathe in fine.

finding.label: Abdomen and Murphy sign
finding.text: Soft. Minimal right upper quadrant tenderness to deep palpation, no guarding, no mass. Negative Murphy sign between attacks.

choices.text: Perform a digital rectal exam
choices.feedback: A rectal exam adds nothing to upper abdominal pain with normal bowels.
choices.patientCue: For my gallbladder, doc? Say it simple, why do you need that?

rounds.prompt: No labs were shared and his scan report is not on the chart. What do you do next?

choices.text: Order a CT of the abdomen and pelvis
choices.feedback: Ultrasound is the test for gallstones; CT adds radiation and misses many stones.
choices.patientCue: Sure. That's why I'm here.

finding.label: CT abdomen and pelvis
finding.text: No acute abnormality. Gallstones not well seen on CT.

choices.text: Order a CBC, basic metabolic panel, liver tests and a right upper quadrant ultrasound
choices.feedback: Baseline labs check kidney function on lisinopril, liver tests screen for a duct stone, and ultrasound confirms the stones.
choices.patientCue: Sure. That's why I'm here.

finding.label: Labs and ultrasound
finding.text: CBC: White count 6.8, hemoglobin 14.6, platelets 232. Normal. BMP: Sodium 140, potassium 4.5, creatinine 1.0, glucose 104. Normal kidney function. LFTs: Total bilirubin 0.8, alkaline phosphatase 90, AST 26, ALT 30. Normal. Ultrasound: Multiple gallstones up to 15 mm. Gallbladder wall 3 mm, no pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy sign negative. Common bile duct 4 mm.

choices.text: Order a right upper quadrant ultrasound only
choices.feedback: Ultrasound confirms the stones, but with no labs on file you still need kidney function and liver tests before surgery.
choices.patientCue: They did a scan. The doctor said a surgeon would explain it. Sure, again if you need it.

finding.label: Right upper quadrant ultrasound
finding.text: Multiple gallstones up to 15 mm. Gallbladder wall 3 mm, no pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy sign negative. Common bile duct 4 mm.

choices.text: Order a lipase and a urinalysis
choices.feedback: Lipase and urinalysis chase unlikely diagnoses and miss the kidney and liver labs he needs.
choices.patientCue: Sure. That's why I'm here.

rounds.prompt: Recurrent meal-triggered attacks, a benign exam, normal labs and stones on ultrasound. What is the diagnosis?

choices.text: Acute cholecystitis
choices.feedback: Short attacks, no fever, a negative Murphy sign and a thin wall without fluid exclude cholecystitis.
choices.patientCue: I'm a bus driver, doc, say it simple. Is that my gallbladder?

choices.text: Choledocholithiasis
choices.feedback: Normal liver tests, a 4 mm duct and no dark urine or jaundice make a duct stone unlikely.
choices.patientCue: That's a mouthful. My doctor just said my gallbladder.

choices.text: Gallstones
choices.feedback: Stones are present, but the diagnosis should name them as symptomatic, causing biliary colic, since that is what justifies surgery.
choices.patientCue: So it's like a clogged filter, like I figured?

choices.text: Symptomatic cholelithiasis (biliary colic)
choices.feedback: Stereotyped postprandial right upper quadrant attacks with stones and no inflammation or duct obstruction is biliary colic.
choices.patientCue: Okay. So it's my gallbladder causing the attacks. Like a flat tire, you can drive on it a while, but you know it's coming.

choices.text: Recommend elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy, with cefazolin prophylaxis and identity confirmed at the time out
choices.feedback: Recurrent uncomplicated biliary colic is treated with elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and a remote rash allows cefazolin.
choices.patientCue: Okay. Let's get it done. How long before I can carry the cooler?

choices.text: Admit him today for an urgent laparoscopic cholecystectomy
choices.feedback: The operation is right, but he is pain-free with no inflammation, so it should be scheduled electively.
choices.patientCue: Today? Tell you the truth, doc, I feel fine right now. Does it have to be today?

choices.text: Refer for ERCP to clear the bile duct first
choices.feedback: ERCP is for a suspected duct stone, and his liver tests and duct size put him at low risk.
choices.patientCue: I don't know what that is, doc. Say it simple.

choices.text: Advise a low-fat diet and see him again if the attacks get worse
choices.feedback: After five or six attacks, watchful waiting risks cholecystitis, a duct stone or pancreatitis.
choices.patientCue: I've already been eating less fried stuff, doc. The attacks keep coming.

closingLine: Okay. Let's get it done. Do I keep taking my blood pressure pill before? And I'd like it done before my grandson Mateo's birthday in December.
